source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use sunscreen as the primary protection for the infant because shade and clothing provide insufficient ultraviolet protection.","B":"Provide brief direct midday sun exposure each day because infants younger than 6 months are less susceptible to sunburn.","C":"Apply an adult sunscreen routinely to all exposed skin before using shade or protective clothing.","D":"Keep the 4-month-old out of direct sunlight when possible, use shade and protective clothing, and ask the pediatrician before applying sunscreen."}}
source_row.rationale: FDA guidance recommends keeping infants younger than 6 months out of direct sunlight, using shade and protective clothing, and consulting a pediatrician before applying sunscreen to this age group. Sunscreen is not generally recommended as the primary protection for young infants.
source_row.source_detail: For infants younger than 6 months, FDA recommends shade and protective clothing and advises consulting a pediatrician before sunscreen use. source_row.source_name: FDA — Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually
source_row.stem: A parent asks how to protect a 4-month-old infant from ultraviolet exposure. Which teaching is most appropriate?
